title: March 5—the Day We Turn Our Tears into a Shield
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement. Letter-specific notes: 1. **TESO** is the Tamil Eelam Supporters Organisation; the acronym is retained throughout the translation. 2. **arapporattam** is rendered in the body as a peaceful moral protest; the source uses the Dravidian-movement term for a principled, non-violent political struggle. 3. The letter recounts graphic allegations of wartime killing and sexual violence. They remain explicitly presented as the claims, reports and recollections contained in Kalaignar's source text; this archival translation does not independently verify them. 4. The names and quotations of Kuttimani and Thangathurai are preserved as presented in the audited Tamil source.
paragraphs: On 20 February 2013 itself, I issued a detailed statement about how brutally the army of Sinhala President Rajapaksa had shot and killed Balachandran, the younger son of Liberation Tigers leader Velupillai Prabhakaran—a child of only twelve. It was not I alone. Everyone with a heart was shaken and shed tears at the destruction of that young shoot, and expressed their severe condemnation of the Sinhala government.

The horrific sight of Balachandran's killing was shown to journalists at the Constitution Club in Delhi through the documentary No Fire Zone produced by London-based Channel 4. Director Callum Macrae, who made and released two documentaries under the title Sri Lanka's Killing Fields, also produced and directed this film. It was named No Fire Zone in remembrance of the Sinhala army's brutal attacks inside areas designated as zones where attacks should not be carried out, killing thousands of Eelam Tamil people without mercy. The documentary has brought out many further pieces of evidence of what the writer describes as unforgivable war crimes committed by the Rajapaksa government.

Newspapers and television organisations have described the documentary as containing scenes of a mother and child lying dead together; Eelam Tamils being treated in hospitals after losing parts of their bodies; innocent women stripped and shot dead; many women being loaded into a lorry on suspicion that they were female Tigers; Colonel Ramesh, one of the LTTE commanders captured by the Sinhala army, lying dead with his face disfigured; the young woman Isaipriya, described as a female-Tiger commander, being sexually abused and killed by the Sinhala army; men stripped, blindfolded, their hands tied behind their backs and shot in the back; and bodies of people killed in bombing lying scattered. When merely reading about these images makes our hearts tremble and ache, what would become of us if we saw them all? We can only agonise, wondering why Tamils ever had to go to the island of Sri Lanka to be subjected to such cruelties.

Successive pieces of evidence have emerged in the documentary as truths that cannot be concealed, supporting the charge that the Sinhala government committed war crimes no person with a heart could accept.
The killers did not even spare children; they pointed guns as though extending toys and shot them dead! What further evidence could be needed that blatant human-rights violations took place?

There is further evidence, the letter says, that inhuman cruelties continue in Sri Lanka. The international human-rights organisation Human Rights Watch prepared a 140-page report after direct investigation in Sri Lanka. It contains details from direct interviews with 75 Tamils who said they had been subjected to sexual violence. Speaking about the report, the organisation's Asia director, Adams, said that sexual violence by members of the Sri Lankan military against Tamil women and men who had been arrested and were in custody was beyond counting, and that these were not merely atrocities committed during the war but incidents continuing to the present day.

The honour of Tamil women has been cast to the winds in Eelam. Tamil women whose chastity was violated were thrown naked and dead into the streets. In Tamil Eelam, thousands of Tamil women—on a scale said to be without parallel elsewhere in the world—have lost their husbands and live as widows. Sinhala soldiers are said to mock them by saying they will keep them as concubines. Were there not even shop signs saying, “Tamil flesh for sale”?

Was a husband not tied to a tree while his wife was sexually assaulted before his very eyes? I recall an incident said to have occurred in Eelam. Bhaskaran was a Tamil man. He was tied to a tree, while his wife was stripped and raped in the middle of the street. The perpetrators did not stop there. The naked woman was hung upside down between two areca palms, one leg tied to one tree and the other leg to the other tree, with the tops of the palms bound together. The tops were then suddenly cut loose. As the trees sprang apart, her body was torn in two and fell—all before the eyes of her husband Bhaskaran. Did this happen in Sri Lanka or not? Has it all been forgotten?

Some years ago, after learning of atrocities in Sri Lanka, the United States sent a three-member team there to ascertain the facts. The team submitted a report at the U.N. Human Rights Council meeting last March saying that abuses had indeed taken place. During discussion of that report, Sri Lanka denied all the allegations and said relief work was under way.

To find out whether even those claims were true, the United States sent another team to Sri Lanka. That team too reported that it was not satisfied with the relief work. It is on that basis that the United States has prepared another resolution. Debate on that resolution is to take place in Geneva at the end of March, followed by a vote on what action should be taken.

Are these atrocities in Sri Lanka something that began only today or yesterday? From the time of Thanthai Selva, have not Eelam Tamil people—tender shoots, buds, flowers, unripe fruit and ripe fruit—been falling and perishing? It was because Sinhala chauvinism had already risen to the point where a person could be attacked and killed simply for being Tamil that more than fifty prisoners, including Kuttimani, Thangathurai and Jegan, were tortured and killed in prison; that became the opening mark of genocide. In 1978–79, when I and a few friends were talking on the Chennai seafront with Thangathurai, Kuttimani and some other freedom fighters, they showed me their feet by torchlight. Their soles were covered with blisters. We asked why. They said that while travelling secretly to reach Tamil Nadu, they had come barefoot because the sound of footwear might betray them to their enemies.
That Kuttimani, Thangathurai, Jegan and thirty-four other Tamil Eelam liberation fighters were killed inside prison itself.

When Kuttimani and Thangathurai were sentenced to death, Thangathurai said: “If we die, your laws and rules will not be able to control the Tamil Eelam that will arise in the future.” In that same court Kuttimani said: “I am not a coward who fears death! After you hang and kill me, take out my eyes and transplant them into the eyes of a blind young man in Eelam. Even if I cannot see the free Tamil Eelam that will blossom in the future, I will rejoice by seeing it through my eyes transplanted into that young man.” The letter recalls the cruelty of such young men being killed within the prison cells, their eyes gouged out, and the attackers asking, “Was it with these eyes that you wanted to see Tamil Eelam?” before throwing the eyes down and trampling on them.

It is to bring all these sufferings to the attention of the people of our country and remind them, and to make them recognise Sinhala-racist President Rajapaksa as an international war criminal, that the TESO consultative meeting held at Anna Arivalayam on 25 February 2013 decided and announced an arapporattam—a peaceful moral protest—to lay siege to the Sri Lankan Deputy High Commission in Chennai on March 5, and a democratic protest in front of Parliament in Delhi on the same day.

On behalf of the DMK and the TESO movement we have already conducted many forms of protest against the cruelties taking place in Sri Lanka. With just one day's notice we have gathered more than five lakh people and held a march. We have conducted hunger strikes, human chains and demonstrations dressed in black. Why, Perasiriyar and I even resigned our positions as Members of the Legislative Assembly. We took to the United Nations a petition signed by more than one crore people. We have twice lost governments over the Sri Lankan issue. I therefore ask you, with the right that comes from our shared struggle, to make the March 5 siege protest too a complete success, just as Udanpirappus have made every previous protest successful.

As always, I ask not only DMK members but also the Udanpirappus of the movements that are part of TESO to come in ranks and participate. March 5—the siege protest opposite the Sri Lankan mission—do not forget to take part. March 5 is the day to reveal once again to the world the anguish in our hearts; March 5 is the day to turn our tears into a shield to protect the Eelam Tamils.
